1352.title: Just sitting
1352.hook: a cushion, a wall, and no technique at all: Zen's sitting practice
1352.howItsDone: In Soto Zen, practitioners sit zazen as shikantaza, upright with eyes open and no object of focus, often in a meditation hall together and at set times of day.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the science block with the line solid and light: keep what's solid, hold the rest lightly. Now a new block opens, the world's schools of practice, starting with Zen.

A round cushion on the floor. A plain wall a few feet away. Someone sits down, crosses their legs, rests their hands in their lap, and then nothing else happens. No counting the breath. No phrase to repeat. No candle, no picture to hold in the mind. A person just sits there, awake. That can sound like waiting for the real thing to start. In one Zen school, this is the real thing, and the Japanese teacher Dogen gave it a name almost too plain to be a teaching: just sitting.
screen: `A CUSHION. A WALL.` → `NO TECHNIQUE AT ALL.` → `JUST SITTING.`

segments.voice: Back on day one hundred three, the word zen turned out to mean meditation. Zazen is Zen's word for seated meditation, and Dogen's name for the way he taught it was shikantaza, usually put into English as just sitting. First, it has no technique. The last block met practices with a job to do: count the breath, note the thought, scan the body. Just sitting sets the jobs down. Second, the body does the work. In his short guide to zazen, Dogen's instructions are physical and plain: sit on a cushion, cross the legs, fold the hands, keep the back upright, don't lean left or right, forward or back. Eyes stay open, resting gently. Breath goes quietly through the nose. Third, thoughts. They will come. Dogen doesn't say to fight them or to follow them. His advice, in paraphrase: when a thought arises, notice it, and in the noticing it goes. He passes on an old exchange, too: asked what you think about while sitting, a teacher answers, roughly, think of not-thinking. And how do you do that? Non-thinking. It's meant to puzzle a little. Fourth, the surprise: for Dogen, sitting isn't a tool for getting enlightenment later. He taught that practice and awakening aren't two separate things; the sitting is already what it's looking for. Hard to hold in your head, which may be why he kept handing people a cushion instead of an argument. The Soto school, which traces itself to Dogen, puts just sitting at its heart. Rinzai Zen also sits zazen, and often adds something else to the cushion. That's tomorrow.
screen: `A SITTING WITH NO TECHNIQUE.` · `BACK UPRIGHT, EYES OPEN, BREATH QUIET.` · `A THOUGHT COMES: NOTICE, AND IT GOES.` · `NOT A TOOL. THE SITTING ITSELF.`

segments.voice: On a chair is fine: feet on the floor, back upright but not stiff, hands in your lap, eyes open and resting softly on the floor a little ahead. Breathe through your nose and leave the breath alone; when a thought shows up, notice it, and come back to sitting. There's nothing to get right, and another day, ten minutes is a good next step.
Zazen. Seated meditation in Zen. In Dogen's way of teaching it, just sitting, with nothing added. Today's word.
Your line: just sitting. Nothing added to it, and nothing missing from it. Until tomorrow.

1353.title: The koan
1353.hook: two hands clap and there's a sound. what is the sound of one hand?
1353.howItsDone: In Rinzai Zen, a teacher assigns a koan, the student works on it during and between sittings, and brings responses to the teacher in private interviews.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: zazen, seated meditation, done Dogen's way as just sitting. Your line was just sitting.

Clap. Two hands meet and there's a sound. Easy. The Japanese Zen teacher Hakuin put a question to his students, in effect: that's two hands. What is the sound of one hand? A student's mind goes straight to work. A wave in the air? Silence? A trick about physics? Each answer gets carried to the teacher, and, the way this practice works, each one can be sent back. Not that. Try again. Questions like this look exactly like riddles, and they aren't.
screen: `TWO HANDS: A SOUND.` → `ONE HAND: WHAT SOUND?` → `NOT THAT. TRY AGAIN.`

segments.voice: A koan is a short story, question or exchange that a Zen student works on in practice. First, it isn't a riddle. A riddle has a clever answer waiting at the end, and once you find it, you're done. A koan pushes back against cleverness. Explanations about air and silence miss the point, and the teacher can tell. Second, it lives in the sitting. In Rinzai Zen, the school Hakuin belonged to, a student often sits zazen with a koan. The question goes onto the cushion, and off it too: walking, eating, working, it rides along. Third, it gets tested face to face. The student brings a response to the teacher in a private meeting. The teacher may accept it, or ring a bell and send the student back to sit. Teachers in this tradition say they're looking for something lived, not something argued. Fourth, what it's for. Hakuin wrote about great doubt: holding the question so fully that the usual busy thinking runs out of road. In his teaching, past the bottom of that doubt is awakening. So a koan isn't a test of intelligence; it's more like a stone in the shoe that keeps you walking differently. Some readers outside Zen meet koans in books as wise sayings to admire. Inside Rinzai practice they're closer to a tool you work with, with a teacher, for a long time. Koans were gathered into collections, with short comments from teachers. Tomorrow, the one that opens The Gateless Gate.
screen: `NOT A RIDDLE.` · `IT RIDES ALONG ON THE CUSHION.` · `TESTED FACE TO FACE.` · `GREAT DOUBT, THEN AWAKENING.`

segments.voice: Sit the way you did yesterday, upright, eyes soft and open, and let the question in quietly: what is the sound of one hand? Don't answer it; when your mind offers an explanation, set it down and ask again, letting the question sit in the body more than the head. If you get bored or puzzled, that's part of it too.

1354.title: Zhaozhou's mu
1354.hook: a monk asks if a dog has Buddha-nature. the teacher answers with one syllable.
1354.howItsDone: In Rinzai and some other Zen lineages, students are often given mu as a first koan and work on it during sitting, breathing the syllable and bringing their response to a teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: koan, a question that won't let you be clever. Your line was one hand.

A monk bows to the old Chinese teacher Zhaozhou, the same teacher who once sent a newcomer to wash his bowl, back on day forty-seven. This monk has heard the teaching that living beings have Buddha-nature, the capacity to wake up. So he points at the humblest example he can find. Does a dog have Buddha-nature, or not? The expected answer is yes. Zhaozhou says one syllable: mu. In Chinese and Japanese, it means something like no, or not, or there isn't. A question, a single word, and a puzzle that has kept students sitting ever since.
screen: `DOES A DOG HAVE BUDDHA-NATURE?` → `THE EXPECTED ANSWER: YES.` → `ZHAOZHOU: MU.`

segments.voice: In the collection called The Gateless Gate, gathered by the Chinese teacher Wumen, Zhaozhou's mu is the first case. First, the surface. Read flatly, Zhaozhou seems to contradict the teaching the monk was repeating. If everything has Buddha-nature, why say no? That's exactly the hook: the no doesn't fit, so the mind can't file it away. Second, it isn't a vote on dogs. Zen teachers say the point isn't a yes or no about animals. Some records even have Zhaozhou answering the same question differently on another day, with a yes. That alone suggests the word is doing something other than giving information. Third, Wumen's comment. Right after the case, he tells the student how to work on it, in vivid pictures. In paraphrase: put your whole body into this mu, day and night. Don't take it as nothing, and don't take it as the opposite of something. It's like swallowing a red-hot iron ball you can't spit out. Fourth, what's left. Wumen's promise, again paraphrased, is that when the work ripens, inside and outside become one, and the student knows it the way someone who can't speak knows their own dream. So mu ends up less like an answer and more like a door. That's why the book is called The Gateless Gate.
screen: `THE FIRST CASE IN THE GATELESS GATE.` · `THE NO DOESN'T FIT.` · `NOT A VOTE ON DOGS.` · `A RED-HOT IRON BALL.`

segments.voice: Sit upright, eyes soft, and let the breath come in on its own. On each out-breath, silently let the syllable ride all the way out, muuu, without thinking what it means or making it yes or no; when the mind wanders, the next out-breath is another mu. Another day, you might try three minutes.
Zhaozhou's mu. A teacher's one-syllable answer, something like no, to a monk's question about a dog. The first case in The Gateless Gate. Today's word.
Your line: mu. One syllable, breathed until it stops being a word about something and is just there. See you tomorrow.

1355.title: Beginner's mind
1355.hook: the expert sees few possibilities. the beginner sees many.
1355.howItsDone: Zen teachers speak of beginner's mind as a way to approach each sitting and each ordinary task freshly, and students are encouraged to keep it however long they have practiced.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: Zhaozhou's mu, one syllable that doesn't fit the question. Your line was mu.

Shoelaces. Somebody tied a pair this morning without a thought about loops or tension or which hand goes where. Now watch a small child do it for the first time. Tongue out. Every loop is an event. The lace slips, and it's fascinating. Same shoes, same laces, two different experiences of the same knot. The adult is faster, and that's useful. But somewhere along the way, the knot stopped being interesting. Back on day forty-three, a teacup overflowed to show a mind too full to learn. Today, the word it pointed to, up close.
screen: `A KNOT TIED WITHOUT A THOUGHT.` → `A CHILD'S FIRST KNOT.` → `THE MIND THAT'S NEW AT THINGS.`

segments.voice: Shoshin is the Japanese word usually put into English as beginner's mind. First, the line that carried it. Shunryu Suzuki, a Japanese Soto Zen teacher who taught in San Francisco, opened a collection of his talks, Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, with an idea that can be paraphrased like this: a beginner's mind holds many possibilities, and an expert's holds only a few. Second, what the expert loses. Knowing how something goes is a shortcut. You stop looking because you already know. That saves time, and it quietly closes doors. A full mind has a hard time noticing what's actually in front of it. Third, what it isn't. Beginner's mind isn't pretending to know nothing, or throwing skill away. It can belong to someone who's sat zazen every day for decades. Suzuki's point, in paraphrase, was that the practice is to keep the beginner's mind, not to graduate from it. Fourth, why Zen cares. Zen practice repeats itself on purpose: the same cushion, the same posture, the same breath. Without beginner's mind, that's a rut. With it, each sitting can be a first sitting. It ties back to the koans, too: mu won't open for someone who already knows the answer. On an ordinary Tuesday, beginner's mind might be as plain as listening to a friend tell a story you've heard before, and actually hearing it.
screen: `MANY POSSIBILITIES, OR FEW.` · `THE EXPERT STOPS LOOKING.` · `NOT FORGETTING YOUR SKILL.` · `EACH SITTING, A FIRST SITTING.`

segments.voice: Hold out one hand, palm up, and look at it as if you'd never seen a hand before: the lines, the color, how the fingers bend and where. Then close your eyes and feel it from the inside, warmth, tingling, weight, and when the mind says it's just my hand, notice that voice and look again. If you'd rather, take one breath as if it were your first.
Shoshin. Beginner's mind. Meeting even the familiar with open eyes, without throwing away what you know. Today's word.
Your line: beginner's mind. Skill kept, door left open. Go gently, and come back tomorrow.

1356.title: Work as Zen
1356.hook: an old cook drying mushrooms in the hot sun: in Zen monasteries, the work period is practice too
1356.howItsDone: In Zen monasteries and practice centers, residents keep a daily work period, cleaning, cooking or gardening, often in silence, as part of their training.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: shoshin, beginner's mind, skill kept and door left open. Your line was beginner's mind.

Midday, a Chinese monastery, and the sun is brutal. An old monk with a bent back is out in the courtyard with no hat, spreading mushrooms to dry, sweating. A visitor from Japan, Dogen, the same Dogen who began this week, stops and asks: why not have a helper do this? The old cook answers, in effect: other people are not me. And why not wait until it's cooler? If not now, when? Dogen writes that he had nothing to say back. He tells the story in his instructions for the monastery cook.
screen: `AN OLD COOK, DRYING MUSHROOMS.` → `OTHERS ARE NOT ME.` → `IF NOT NOW, WHEN?`

segments.voice: Samu is the Japanese Zen word for the work period: cleaning, cooking, sweeping, weeding, done as practice. Back on day forty-seven, Zhaozhou sent a monk to wash his bowl; samu builds that idea into the day. First, what it is. In a Zen monastery the day isn't only sitting. There are set times for physical work, treated as part of the training, not a break from it, often done without chatter, with the attention the cushion asks for. Second, an old saying. Tradition says the Chinese teacher Baizhang kept working in the fields even when he was old. His worried students hid his tools. He refused to eat, and said, as the story goes: a day without work is a day without food. Whether or not it happened just that way, Zen still repeats the saying. Third, the cook's answer. Other people are not me. He wasn't refusing help out of pride. His practice was this task, in his own hands; sending it away would send away his practice. And if not now, when: the moment to pay attention is the one you're in, even if it's hot. Fourth, off the cushion. Washing a pan can be zazen with your hands moving. In his instructions for the cook, Dogen asks, in paraphrase, that rice and water be handled with the care you'd give your own eyes. Nobody has to live in a monastery to try that with a sink full of dishes.
screen: `SAMU: THE WORK PERIOD AS PRACTICE.` · `A DAY WITHOUT WORK, A DAY WITHOUT FOOD.` · `OTHERS ARE NOT ME.` · `THE CUSHION, WITH YOUR HANDS MOVING.`

segments.voice: Find one small thing within reach that needs care, a cup to wash, a table to wipe, a pair of shoes to line up, and do it slowly, feeling its weight, the water's temperature, the cloth under your hand. When your mind runs ahead to what's next, come back to this one motion; if you can't move where you are, tidy one thing in your pocket or bag. Another day, ten minutes of cleaning this way is a good next step.
Samu. The Zen work period, cleaning, cooking, tending, done as practice, with the same attention as sitting. Today's word.
Your line: work is practice. Not someone else, and not later: this one, now. Rest easy.

1357.title: The teacher
1357.hook: a flower held up, a smile, and nothing said: Zen stresses face-to-face teaching
1357.howItsDone: Zen students usually practice under a teacher, meeting in private interviews to bring questions and koan responses, and Zen schools trace their teachers in lineages.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: samu, the work period, and an old cook in the sun. Your line was work is practice.

Zen tells a story about a sermon with no words in it. The Buddha stands before a gathering of his followers, and instead of speaking, he lifts a single flower and turns it in his fingers. Nobody knows what to make of it. Except one disciple, Mahakashyapa, who smiles. And the Buddha, the story says, declares that something has passed to him, something the words of a sermon couldn't hold. A flower, a smile, and the beginning of a lineage.
screen: `A FLOWER, HELD UP.` → `ONE DISCIPLE SMILES.` → `SOMETHING PASSES, WITHOUT WORDS.`

segments.voice: Zen puts great weight on the teacher, and on meeting face to face. First, the flower. The story is told as a case in The Gateless Gate, the same collection that opens with Zhaozhou's mu. Zen tells it as its own origin story, and its point is the picture: understanding passing between two people, directly. Second, the old verse. Tradition attributes to Bodhidharma, the teacher said to have carried Zen to China, a short description of the school, in paraphrase: a special transmission outside the scriptures, not depending on words and letters, pointing straight at the mind. Third, the catch. That doesn't make Zen against books. This whole week has leaned on them: Dogen's writings, The Gateless Gate, Hakuin, Suzuki's talks. The point is that books aren't enough. A book can't see you. It can't tell when your answer to a koan is clever and when it's real. That's the teacher's job, in the private meeting we met earlier this week, where a student brings a response and a teacher looks back. Fourth, the line of people. Zen schools keep lineages: chains of teachers and students, each taught by someone who was taught by someone. Tradition says Dogen crossed the sea to China in search of a teacher; that journey is how he met the old cook. Which leaves a plain question: who, in your own life, has taught you something face to face that no page could?
screen: `A FLOWER AND A SMILE.` · `OUTSIDE THE SCRIPTURES, NOT IN WORDS.` · `A BOOK CAN'T SEE YOU.` · `A LINE OF TEACHERS, PERSON TO PERSON.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who taught you something in person: a grandparent at a stove, a coach, a boss who showed you how, a friend who said the hard thing to your face. Let their face come clear, and ask what they passed on that you couldn't have read. If you pray, hold them in your prayer; if not, just sit with them a moment, face to face in memory.
The teacher. In Zen, the person who meets you face to face, and passes on what words alone can't carry. Today's word.

1358.title: Four foundations
1358.hook: a to-do list for attention, four lines long: body, feelings, mind, and what the mind meets
1358.howItsDone: In Theravada Buddhism, meditation teachers draw on the Satipatthana Sutta, and students practice mindfulness of breath and body, feeling tones, states of mind and the teachings as they show up in experience.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: the teacher, and a flower held up in silence. Your line was face to face. That closed a week of Zen; today the path crosses to the Theravada schools.

One of the Buddha's discourses hands its listeners something like a to-do list for attention, four lines long. Not a list of beliefs. A list of places to look. One: the body. Two: feelings. Three: the mind itself. Four: the things the mind meets and works with. Each line opens into detailed instructions, and the whole is framed as a path. Back on day seven hundred sixty-five, this same discourse took us to a charnel ground; today, the whole map. It's the Satipatthana Sutta, and in the Theravada schools of Southeast Asia and Sri Lanka, meditation teachers draw on it.
screen: `FOUR PLACES TO LOOK.` → `BODY, FEELINGS, MIND, WHAT THE MIND MEETS.` → `THE SATIPATTHANA SUTTA.`

segments.voice: Satipatthana is the Pali word for these four foundations, or establishings, of mindfulness. The sutta sits in the Middle Length Discourses, number ten. First, the body. It starts with breathing: a meditator goes to a quiet place, sits, and knows a long breath as long and a short breath as short. Then it widens to the postures, walking, standing, sitting, lying down, and to ordinary actions like eating and dressing, done knowing what you're doing. Second, feelings. Here feeling doesn't mean emotion. It means the simple tone of an experience: pleasant, unpleasant, or neither. The meditator just knows which one is present. Third, the mind. Angry or not? Scattered or gathered? The instruction isn't to fix it; it's to know it as it is. Fourth, the things the mind meets, in Pali, dhammas. Here the sutta lists teachings to watch in action: hindrances like restlessness and doubt, the factors that lead toward awakening, and the four noble truths. Through all four runs a refrain, in paraphrase: the meditator watches ardent, clearly knowing, and mindful, noticing things arising and passing away. That points straight at tomorrow. Two things worth noticing. Dogen's just sitting set the techniques down; this sutta lays out a careful map. Different schools, different ways in, each with its own teachers. And the list starts with breath and body: the abstract parts come last, after you've learned to feel your own feet.
screen: `ONE: THE BODY, STARTING WITH BREATH.` · `TWO: PLEASANT, UNPLEASANT, OR NEITHER.` · `THREE: KNOW THE MIND AS IT IS.` · `FOUR: WHAT THE MIND MEETS.`

segments.voice: Give each foundation about half a minute: feel one breath, long or short, and where you touch the chair; then ask whether this moment is pleasant, unpleasant or neither. Know whether the mind is busy or quiet, scattered or gathered, without fixing it. Last, notice what it meets, restlessness, doubt or a little calm, and watch it come and change.
Satipatthana. The four foundations of mindfulness: body, feelings, mind, and the things the mind meets. Today's word.
Your line: four foundations. Body, feeling, mind, and what the mind meets. Back tomorrow, same hill.
